rv.q: Jonas has crafted a thoughtful, truthful meditation on parenthood, community, and the stories we tell to survive.
Centered by Dee Pelletier amid the true ensemble cast, A Woman Among Women swims through puzzling experimental choices before it lands with a bang.
It’s an ambitious mission, and this particular play has a compelling story to tell. It also has a striking “new form,” like Treplev’s play, that can get in the way of the storytelling.
A Woman Among Women, though, frustrates more than excites.
The bumper crop of plays about plays is becoming tiresome.

That said, to my old-school taste, the ambitious A Woman Among Women registers mostly as a terribly talky, at times even tedious, theater exercise that fails to engage pity or any emotion other than occasional confusion.
And while I applaud the effort, the work falls well short of its ambitions.
A Woman Among Women is an exceptional piece of writing, both in the context of All My Sons, and as a standalone piece.
These are fascinating, even important questions — and Jonas poses them with considerable skill.
Frustratingly slow to ignite, but genuinely thought-provoking once it does.

A Woman Among Women is a mixed bag, with acerbic humor, disturbing situations, and a final reckoning that shakes the community to its core, infused with musical numbers that lengthen the show and break the mood and narrative flow with little reason.

cn.t: Jonas's gender-swapped take on Miller's "All My Sons" earns mixed reviews, with critics praising Pelletier's performance and the ambitious feminist reimagining, but faulting a slow-paced first two acts that undercut the dramatic payoff.

vr.q: While the crux of the piece does end up coming together and the exploration of morality and matriarchy is ripe with intrigue, it takes too long to get there.
